w: Hakons Hall opened on 1 February 1993 at Stampesletta, built for ice hockey at the 1994 Winter Olympics. It seats 11,500, Norway's largest handball and ice hockey venue, and later hosted the 1994 Paralympics ceremonies and the Junior Eurovision Song Contest 2004. It now houses the Norwegian Olympic Museum.
s: 11,500-seat arena that hosted 1994 Olympic ice hockey
_facts: Opened 1 February 1993, cost 238 million NOK
Built for 1994 Winter Olympics ice hockey
Capacity 11,500, Norway's largest handball/ice hockey venue

w: Maihaugen, formally De Sandvigske Samlinger pa Maihaugen, is one of Lillehammer's most-visited attractions. With close to 200 buildings gathered on site, it ranks as one of Northern Europe's largest open-air museums and one of Norway's largest cultural facilities overall.
s: Almost 200 buildings, a huge open-air museum
_facts: Formal name: De Sandvigske Samlinger pa Maihaugen
Close to 200 buildings on site
One of Northern Europe's largest open-air museums
One of Norway's largest cultural facilities

w: Garmo Stave Church stands inside the Maihaugen open-air museum in Lillehammer Municipality, one of nearly 200 buildings on the site. Despite that setting, it ranks among the most-visited stave churches in all of Norway, drawing visitors without a trip to its original parish.
s: A stave church at Maihaugen, among Norway's best-visited
_facts: Located at the Maihaugen open-air museum

w: Hafjell, a village and ski resort in Oyer Municipality, hosted the alpine giant slalom and slalom at the 1994 Winter Olympics, while the speed events ran at nearby Kvitfjell. The resort has since staged World Cup slalom and giant slalom races, most recently a women's event in 2006 and men's finals in 1996.
s: 1994 Olympic alpine venue still hosting World Cup races
_facts: Hosted 1994 Winter Olympics giant slalom and slalom

w: Founded in 1921 on a gift from merchant Einar Lunde, Lillehammer Art Museum grew from Lunde's Matisse-school paintings, a 19th-century collection donated in 1958, and Jon Dobloug's 2008 gift of 1980s-90s works. Its 1963 galleries and 1992 Snohetta extension, Flygelet, served as the 1994 Olympics' main cultural venue.

_facts: Founded 1921 from Einar Lunde's gift

w: The Norwegian Olympic Museum at Maihaugen traces the Games from antiquity to today, weighted toward the 1952 Oslo and 1994 Lillehammer Olympics, through over 7,000 objects. King Harald V and Queen Sonja opened it in Hakons Hall in 1997; it reopened at Maihaugen in 2016, the only such museum in northern Europe.
s: 7,000-item museum covering every Olympics, old and new
_facts: Opened 27 November 1997 by King Harald V and Queen Sonja
Reopened at Maihaugen in 2016
Over 7,000 Olympic items
Only northern European museum covering the full Olympic history

w: Hunderfossen Familiepark, north of Lillehammer, opened in 1984 and now draws over 275,000 visitors each summer to more than 60 attractions, many themed on Norwegian folk tales collected by Asbjornsen and Moe. It also runs a winter park each Feb-March, and appeared in Netflix's Lilyhammer and the film Troll.

_facts: Opened 1984; over 275,000 summer visitors

w: Aulestad, a farm in Follebu, was home to Nobel Prize-winning author Bjornstjerne Bjornson and his wife Karoline from 1875 until his death in 1910. Still owned by the Bjornson family, it joined the Sandvig Collections in 1934 and opened as a museum in 1935, now run alongside Maihaugen and the Norwegian Olympic Museum.

_facts: Home of Nobel laureate Bjornstjerne Bjornson, 1875-1910

w: Faaberg Church, a red wooden cruciform building designed by Svend Traaseth, has served its parish since 1727 and seats about 292. Beside it stands the Faaberg stone, a runestone believed to be one of three monoliths that once stood near the church - an 18th-century parish church paired with a pre-Christian inscription.

_facts: Built 1727 in cruciform design by Svend Traaseth
Seats about 292
Located beside the Faaberg runestone

w: Follebu Church has stood in its village since 1260, built as a white stone long-church by an architect whose name was never recorded. It seats about 140 and serves the Follebu parish within the Sor-Gudbrandsdal deanery, one of the oldest buildings still active in the wider Lillehammer area.

_facts: Built in 1260, white stone long-church

w: Birkebeineren Ski Stadium, 3km from central Lillehammer at 485m elevation, was built for the 1994 Winter Olympics at a cost of 83.6 million NOK. Cross-country capacity is 31,000, biathlon 13,500. It has since hosted a Biathlon World Cup, three Cross-Country World Cups, and the 2016 Youth Olympics.
_facts: Built for 1994 Winter Olympics, cost 83.6 million NOK

w: At 1,089 metres, Nevelfjell is the highest point in Lillehammer Municipality, about 11km northeast of town near the Oyer border. On clear days, the summit offers panoramic views across the Jotunheimen and Rondane ranges. Hiking and ski trails climb to the top, where a small cabin, Nevelhytta, shelters walkers.
s: Lillehammer's highest point, views to Jotunheimen
_facts: Highest point in Lillehammer Municipality at 1,089m
About 11km northeast of Lillehammer town

w: Kanthaugen Freestyle Arena, opened in 1992 for the 1994 Winter Olympics, packs three hills into one venue for aerials, moguls and now-defunct ski ballet. Moguls capacity is 12,000, the other two 15,000 each. Norway's national freestyle venue, it hosted the FIS World Cup and 2016 Youth Olympics, beside Lysgardsbakken.

_facts: Opened 1992 for the 1994 Winter Olympics

w: St Mary Church, in Suttestad south of Lillehammer, serves the Catholic parish of western Innlandet, with chapels in Gjovik, Oppa and Dokka. Founded in 1956, the parish worshipped in a private chapel until this building went up in 1970 by architect Carl Corwin, consecrated with relics by Bishop Bernt Eidsvig in 2010.

w: Lillehammer Church, a red brick long-church designed by Henrik Thrap-Meyer, has stood in the town centre since 1882 and seats about 650. It is the parish church for Lillehammer itself and the seat of the Sor-Gudbrandsdal deanery, making it the administrative heart of Church of Norway life across the wider district.

w: Balbergbakken, near Faaberg, opened in 1972 with a K-120 hill plus three smaller jumps, its cost overrunning 1 million NOK. It hosted Norwegian Championships (1973, 1978, 1983); Tom Levorstad set its hill record, 130.5m, in 1981. Slated for the 1994 Olympics, it was passed over for Lysgardsbakken and closed in 1992.
